structure.title: IV. A Test of the Predictions

observations.statement: The introduction frames the paper's contribution as testing whether a machine-learning method can find treatment-effect heterogeneity that ad hoc subgroup search or prespecified interaction terms would miss, positioning it against preregistration and multiple-testing corrections as alternative solutions to the same problem.

The paper explicitly states the unconfoundedness assumption required for the causal forest to produce consistent treatment-effect estimates: treatment assignment must be orthogonal to potential outcomes within each leaf, which the authors argue holds once they condition on randomization block.
The design variant is named explicitly as an application of the causal forest algorithm, implemented with a stated modification to the original causalForest R package.
observations.quote: a version of Wager and Athey's (2015) algorithm with a modification

observations.statement: Randomization is described as block randomization of applicants within applicant pool, age, and geographic blocks for the later trial, with eligibility criteria deliberately changed between the two trials to create variation for testing treatment heterogeneity.

The authors discuss overfitting as the central threat to interpreting differences between in-sample and out-of-sample subgroup comparisons, and describe an adjusted honest-prediction procedure intended to rule it out as an explanation.

Administrative data are drawn from three distinct government sources: a state police agency's arrest records, a school district's enrollment and schooling records, and a state employment security agency's unemployment insurance records, each linked to program applicants.
The unit of observation is the individual youth applicant to a summer employment program, matched across administrative datasets using identifying information such as Social Security numbers.

The analysis pools two separate randomized trials of the same summer jobs program run in different years, exploiting a deliberate change in eligibility criteria between the two trials to generate additional variation for testing heterogeneity.

The authors state that match rates to administrative arrest data do not differ significantly between treatment and control groups, offered as evidence against differential attrition affecting the main test.

The employment outcome is defined only for applicants with a valid employment-matching identifier, and specifications using it are explicitly restricted to that subsample, while the arrest outcome uses the full matched sample.

The hold-out exercise stratifies the random in-sample and out-of-sample split by randomization block, treatment status, and validity of the employment-matching identifier, so both halves preserve the same design features as the full sample.

The two outcomes are a count of violent-crime arrests over a fixed post-assignment window and a binary indicator for any formal employment over a fixed post-program window, the latter defined only among those with non-missing employment records.
Treatment is defined as random assignment to a summer employment program that provides part-time paid work, an adult mentor, and additional programming, with pay set at the prevailing minimum wage.

To limit missing covariate values, such as prior-year wages that are only observed for applicants with a valid employment identifier who worked, the authors construct mutually exclusive categorical indicators observed for every applicant rather than using the underlying continuous measures directly.
A missing gender indicator is imputed using the mean within randomization block for the applicants lacking that value, rather than dropping those observations from the analysis.

Inverse-probability weights based on block-level treatment probabilities are constructed and applied throughout the causal forest procedure, including in the treatment-effect and variance calculations within leaves, to account for treatment probabilities that vary across randomization blocks.

The main results specification includes fixed effects for randomization block and controls for the baseline covariates used to build the causal forest, alongside the treatment indicator interacted with the predicted-sign group.

The results table is organized into three panels applying the same regression specification to the in-sample data, the held-out data, and an adjusted-prediction version of the in-sample data, letting the same specification be compared across the three cases directly.

Table notes state the dependent variables, describe the estimand as intent-to-treat effects, and specify which sample each panel corresponds to, rather than leaving those details to the main text alone.
The table notes state that standard errors are clustered at the individual level.

The authors explicitly state that they do not adjust inference for the fact that the regressors are themselves generated from estimated predictions, describing the construction of uniformly valid standard errors for causal-forest-based regressors as an open methodological question.

Although the introduction discusses modern multiple-testing corrections as an alternative way to search for heterogeneity, the paper does not apply a formal multiple-testing adjustment to its own reported subgroup-equality tests across outcomes and panels.

The comparison of subgroup treatment-effect differences estimated in-sample versus in a held-out sample is used as the paper's central diagnostic for whether the predicted heterogeneity reflects a genuine pattern rather than overfitting.

No separate formal covariate-balance table is presented for the randomized samples; balance is instead addressed only through a statement that administrative-data match rates do not differ significantly by treatment status.
The paper reports a sensitivity check of how held-out-sample performance depends on the particular random split of the data, describing the result qualitatively as varying rather than tabulating it.

As a robustness check on the overfitting explanation, the authors implement an adjusted honest-prediction method that averages each observation's predicted effect only across trees that never used that observation for building or estimation, and compare the resulting subgroup differences to the unadjusted in-sample estimates.

A footnote reports that increasing the minimum number of treatment and control observations required in each leaf reduces but does not eliminate the differential performance between in-sample and out-of-sample subgroup comparisons, and notes it performs worse than the preferred adjustment at detecting out-of-sample heterogeneity.

The authors state, without presenting the underlying figures, that the causal forest's out-of-sample performance varies depending on how the sample is split, flagged as a caveat about the design's sensitivity rather than as a fully reported robustness table.

Treatment-effect heterogeneity is estimated using a machine-learning method that searches over a high-dimensional combination of covariates for each individual, contrasted explicitly with standard approaches that rely on a small number of prespecified interaction terms.

For testing purposes, the continuous predicted individual treatment effect is collapsed into a binary indicator for whether the prediction is positive or negative, rather than used directly as a continuous regressor, which the authors say reduces estimation error near the threshold.

Rather than testing an economic mechanism behind the program's effects, the paper's central empirical exercise validates whether individuals with larger machine-learning-predicted treatment effects actually respond more strongly in a held-out sample, treating this correlation itself as the object of interest.

The authors frame the detected employment heterogeneity as something that standard interaction-effect models with modern multiple-testing corrections would have failed to uncover, benchmarking their method's value against that conventional alternative rather than describing effect sizes in relative or standardized terms.

The authors state that the causal forest is likely to work best with datasets larger than the held-out sample used in this application, presenting sample size as a constraint on the method's performance here.

The adjustment used to separate overfitting from an unlucky sample split is described by the authors as an ad hoc solution that may require further adjustments to the causal forest's theoretical justification and inference, an explicit caveat about their own robustness fix.

When no treatment heterogeneity is detected for one of the two outcomes, the authors list several possible explanations, including homogeneous true effects, unobserved drivers of heterogeneity, limits of the greedy splitting algorithm, and sampling error, without concluding which explanation applies.

All quantitative results are presented in a single table with parenthetical standard errors under each coefficient and reported p-values for subgroup-equality tests, without asterisks marking conventional significance thresholds.
The paper contains no figures; all results are conveyed through prose description and a single formatted table.

The introduction previews the paper's qualitative bottom line, that the machine-learning method can find heterogeneity conventional approaches miss but performs best in larger samples than the one available after holding out data, ahead of presenting any results.

The paper explains the causal forest methodology in general terms in a background section before describing the specific application, data, and outcomes, then walks through the estimation algorithm as an explicit step-by-step procedure aimed at applied researchers unfamiliar with the method.

There is no separate robustness section; the single robustness check addressing overfitting is presented within the results section as part of interpreting the primary in-sample versus out-of-sample comparison.

A footnote directs readers to the article's DOI landing page for additional materials and an author disclosure statement, rather than describing a specific replication package or repository within the main text.

The causal forest software used is named as a modified version of the causalForest R package, obtained as an early beta release directly from one of the method's original developers rather than from a public release.

The underlying administrative records are described as obtained through named government and school-district data providers, consistent with restricted administrative access rather than public-use data, though no formal data-use agreement or access procedure is described in the text.

The introduction discusses committing to a preregistered analysis plan as one way researchers protect against data mining, contrasting it with the paper's own machine-learning approach, but the text does not state whether this specific heterogeneity analysis was itself preregistered.

The authors explicitly frame their finding that causal forest performance depends on sample size as a scaling consideration for applying the method in other settings, suggesting its usefulness may grow with the size of the available dataset rather than being specific to this program.

concordance.paper_says: Outcomes are regressed on treatment interacted with predicted-sign indicators, with baseline covariates and block fixed effects, described as intent-to-treat regressions.
concordance.card_shows: hdfe_ols estimator via Stata's areg command with fe=['blocks'] recorded across the six RCT specifications s1-s6.

concordance.paper_says: Regressions include block fixed effects alongside the baseline covariates used in the causal forest.
concordance.card_shows: fixed_effects=['blocks'] recorded for specifications s1 through s6.

concordance.paper_says: Table notes state standard errors are clustered on individual.
concordance.card_shows: se.cluster_level=['group'] traced from the Stata cluster(group) option in specifications s1-s6.
concordance.note: The paper's stated clustering unit (individual) and the code's cluster variable name (group) do not match textually; group could conceivably be an individual identifier under a different name, but this cannot be confirmed from the card alone.

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors are described as clustered.
concordance.card_shows: se.type='cluster' recorded for all six RCT specifications.

concordance.paper_says: Inverse-probability weights based on block-level treatment probabilities are applied throughout the procedure, including in treatment-effect and variance calculations.
concordance.card_shows: weights=None (null) recorded for the RCT regression specifications s1-s6; weights are only recorded for the two causal-forest-fitting specifications s7 and s8.
concordance.note: The card does not capture the inverse-probability weighting the paper describes for its outcome regressions, only for the forest-fitting calls.

concordance.paper_says: Treatment effects are compared between the subgroup predicted to respond positively and the subgroup predicted to respond negatively, based on the sign of the predicted individual treatment effect.
The full matched sample is randomly split in half, stratified by block, treatment status, and validity of the employment-matching identifier, to create an estimation sample and a held-out sample.
concordance.card_shows: Card records a sample restriction limiting employment specifications to observations with a valid matching identifier (spec_ids s3, s4, s6), but does not record an in-sample/out-of-sample split as a separate sample field.

concordance.paper_says: The in-sample versus out-of-sample comparison of subgroup treatment-effect differences is presented as the paper's central diagnostic for whether predicted heterogeneity reflects genuine signal rather than overfitting.
concordance.card_shows: diagnostic x3 (heterogeneous_treatment_effects), status=observed, describes the paper as validating whether predicted heterogeneity correlates with actual differential responses in a hold-out sample.

concordance.paper_says: No formal covariate balance table is presented; balance is addressed only through a statement that administrative match rates do not differ significantly by treatment status.
concordance.card_shows: diagnostic x1 (balance), status=not_found_in_scope, notes block randomization is documented in code comments but no formal balance table or diagnostic was found in the traced files.

concordance.paper_says: An adjusted honest-prediction method, averaging each observation's prediction only over trees that never used it for building or estimation, is compared against the baseline in-sample estimates as the paper's robustness check for overfitting.
concordance.card_shows: robustness entry labelled alt_se, baseline specifications s1 and s3 versus variant specifications s5 and s6, described as adjusted causal-forest predictions using custom aggregation.
concordance.note: The card's robustness type label (alt_se) does not exactly match the paper's framing of this as an alternative prediction method rather than an alternative standard-error calculation, but the underlying comparison of baseline versus adjusted-prediction specifications matches.

gaps: No preregistration or IRB/consent statement appears in the extracted text for this specific heterogeneity analysis, despite the introduction discussing preregistration as a general alternative approach.

No multiple-testing correction is applied to the paper's own reported subgroup-difference tests, despite the introduction citing multiple-testing adjustments as an alternative solution to ad hoc heterogeneity search.
The online Appendix referenced for the definition of the causal forest's splitting objective function is not part of the extracted text and was not read.
No explicit statement of software version numbers is given beyond describing the causalForest R package as an early beta version.
No formal covariate balance table for the randomized samples appears in the main text; only a statement about equal administrative match rates is given.

reading.note: All five printed pages of this AEA Papers & Proceedings article, including the references page, were read in full; there is no separate appendix within the extracted text. An online Appendix is referenced in the text for the definition of the causal forest's splitting objective function but is not part of this PDF/extracted text and was not read.
